analysis.one_liner: Bans union contracts that require workers to join a union or pay union fees.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have outlawed mandatory union membership and dues agreements nationwide, never received a single committee action after its referral and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act to strike the provisions that let union contracts require workers to join a union or pay union dues and fees as a condition of employment, including payroll deduction of dues for railroad employees. It would apply nationwide, extending right-to-work rules to every state, and would take effect for agreements entered into or renewed after enactment. The bill was introduced by Sen. Rand Paul in February 2019 with 26 Republican cosponsors and never received a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers gain the most: with unions unable to collect fees from all the workers they must represent, union treasuries shrink and collective bargaining pressure on employers weakens. Workers who object to joining a union or paying fees in the roughly half of states that still allow union security agreements would keep their full job without paying. Railway carriers would no longer be required, under certain agreements, to deduct union dues from paychecks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers and workers who avoid union fees

how_it_helps.text: Employers in unionized workplaces gain bargaining leverage: the bill removes the provisions of the National Labor Relations Act that allow a union and an employer to agree that employees must join the union or pay fees to keep their jobs, which shrinks the union funds and membership that back contract negotiations.

Workers who do not want to belong to a union could no longer be required to pay dues or fees under a union security agreement, anywhere in the country, and could no longer face payroll deduction of dues as a condition of employment in the railroad industry.
Railroad carriers would be freed from the Railway Labor Act provision allowing agreements that require payroll deduction of union dues or fees as a condition of employment.

analysis.who_pays: Organized labor pays first: unions would still be legally required to represent every worker in a unionized workplace but could no longer charge nonmembers for that representation, cutting dues revenue and weakening their ability to bargain and organize. Workers who rely on union representation share the cost, because a weaker union has less money and power to win higher wages and benefits. Research on state right-to-work laws generally finds lower wages and benefits in right-to-work states, so workers in unionized sectors bear much of the loss.

drawbacks.text: Under federal labor law, a union that wins an election must represent every worker in the bargaining unit, member or not. The bill keeps that duty but removes the ability to charge nonmembers fees, so workers could receive union representation for free while the union's funding drains away.

Studies of state right-to-work laws find that wages and benefits are lower on average in right-to-work states, and union membership and household incomes tend to fall; a national version would extend those effects to workers in all 50 states, not just the states that chose them.

The strongest good-faith case for the bill is individual choice: no worker should be forced to fund an organization they did not join. The cost an honest supporter must acknowledge is that unions are legally obliged to represent nonmembers, so eliminating required fees removes the only way unions recover the cost of that representation, shifting money from collective worker institutions to employers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The choice argument is real at the level of the individual worker: nobody wants to pay fees to a group they disagree with. But the bill's design is lopsided — it leaves in place the union's legal duty to represent every worker while stripping away the fees that pay for it. In states that already have such laws, the measurable results have been lower union membership and, on average, lower wages. The main beneficiary is not the individual worker but the employer facing a weaker union at the bargaining table, which is why the bill reads as a transfer of power from workers' organizations to employers rather than a neutral expansion of freedom.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the National Right-to-Work Act in the Senate on February 14, 2019, with 16 Republican senators joining as original cosponsors on the bill itself.
Twenty-six Republicans in total signed on as cosponsors; no Democrat or Independent did.

The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day of introduction, and no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — was ever taken on it.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill expired in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor, let alone the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions and the workers they represent came out ahead: existing union security agreements in the states that allow them remain in force, so unions keep fee revenue and bargaining power that the bill would have eliminated. Employers in non-right-to-work states did not get the nationwide regime they would have gained.

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on February 14, 2019.

for.name: 26 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; 16 of them joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee (Chair Lamar Alexander)
against.role: Committee of referral; never acted on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill received no committee action for the rest of the Congress. Notably, the committee's Republican chair let a bill backed by 26 Republicans sit untouched.

against.name: Organized labor (AFL-CIO and allied unions)
against.what_they_did: Opposed national right-to-work legislation as an existential threat to union funding and bargaining power; unions have long campaigned against such bills.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 senators behind the bill were Republicans, no Democrat or Independent cosponsored, and there was never a vote — the bill died quietly in a Republican-run committee rather than on a party-line roll call.

industries.note: Unions would still have to represent every worker in a unionized workplace but could no longer collect fees from nonmembers, cutting their funding and bargaining power. Since union strength is what wins higher wages and benefits for workers, the union's interest here runs alongside ordinary workers' paychecks.
Weaker unions mean less organized pressure for higher wages, better benefits, and workplace rules. The employer's gain in bargaining leverage comes directly out of workers' collective position.

The bill strikes the Railway Labor Act provision allowing agreements that require payroll deduction of union dues as a condition of employment, weakening railroad unions' finances and, with them, their bargaining position against the carriers.
